reading.body:
FORBES-TATE's AI lobbying book is concentrated: two clients, CoreWeave and Universal Music Group, account for 28 of the 42 AI filings, and CoreWeave alone is tied for the largest share.

The client list is the useful signal. A cloud compute provider and a major record label sit at the top, followed by an AI training company, a think tank, a carmaker, and a veterans' nonprofit. That mix is what AI policy looks like from inside a lobbying shop: infrastructure firms defending their buildout, rights holders defending their training data, and everyone else arriving with narrower asks. The filings name one bill, S 2714, and only for 2025 or later, so the legislative footprint recorded here is thin.

The lobbyist roster is broad and shallow. Twenty-two people are named, but only five appear on 20 or more AI filings, and eleven appear on three or fewer. Franklyn Steinberg at 30 and Rachel Miller at 26 carry most of the volume. A firm this size spreads AI work across many hands rather than routing it through one specialist.

What this does not show is position. A filing reports that a client lobbied on an issue, not what it argued, so CoreWeave's 14 filings could be offense or defense and the data cannot say which. It also does not show spending, outcomes, or whether any of these clients coordinate. The compute and power story behind CoreWeave's presence is implied by the client's business, not by anything in the filings themselves.
